Private deployment vs. Dedicated capacity tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~54 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Sophie Larsen (Aurora Procurement), Ethan Park (Aurora Legal), Priya Menon (Aurora Cloud), Noah Rivera (Aurora CTO)

Summary: Negotiation of MSA/DPA, clarification on SLA metrics and credits, customer requested KMS and data residency details, agreed to run a private deployment latency benchmark before final pricing approval.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Maya from Redwood here, Omar also from our solutions team. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Sophie Larsen: Doing well, thanks. Appreciate you making time, we're on a pretty tight procurement window so hoping to wrap this month.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Totally, that's the goal. We got your redlines to the MSA and DPA, saw the SLA concerns, and thought it'd be good to walk through them live. Also, Ethan and Priya, thanks for coming on.
[00:32] Ethan Park: Yeah no problem. I have the legal redlines open. I want to focus first on liability cap language and also subprocessors in the DPA.
[00:40] Omar Patel: Sounds good. Quick heads up — I'll cover the technical bits on jurisdiction, KMS, and options for private deployment or dedicated pools.
[00:50] Noah Rivera: From the CTO side I'll chime in on performance expectations — we've got latency targets for our chat assistant flows, and cost is obviously a major factor.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Great. So first item, liability cap. Your redline proposes an unlimited carve-out for data breach remediation costs and a cap equal to 12 months of fees. We suggested standard mutual liability with carve-outs for willful misconduct.
[01:25] Ethan Park: Right, and we're asking for a higher cap because we operate in finance and regulators track incident remediation costs closely. We can maybe be flexible on the exact multiple but need stronger protection than the standard.
[01:38] Maya Chen: Understood. Historically Redwood's MSA uses a 12 months fees cap with exceptions for gross negligence and willful misconduct, and statutory liabilities. I can escalate a request to legal for a limited increase — probably to 18 months for enterprise deals. I'll need to get approval.
[01:55] Sophie Larsen: That would help. Also on the DPA, the subprocessors list — we need a commitment to notify changes and a mechanism to object to new subprocessors with a reasonable cure period.
[02:08] Omar Patel: We do notify and list major subprocessors in our DPA. There's also an options matrix for customers who need private deployment or dedicated capacity where subprocessors are limited. For hosted API we do have cloud infra providers listed.
[02:25] Priya Menon: For us, the big question is KMS. We need to use our own KMS for keys or a supported HSM provider. The current DPA references encryption at rest but isn't prescriptive on customer-managed keys.
[02:40] Maya Chen: We can support customer-managed keys on Private deployments and in some dedicated setups. For hosted we can integrate with certain KMS providers via bring-your-own-key; I'll confirm the exact list. Omar, can you cover which KMS are supported today?
[02:53] Omar Patel: Sure. Today we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault for dedicated and private control planes. We also have partners for HSM integrations; for fully air-gapped on-prem we offer a package that allows customer keys only. I'll share a doc with spec.
[03:08] Ethan Park: Good. Please add that to the DPA as an appendix or reference so we have that contractual commitment.
[03:15] Maya Chen: Noted. Next, SLA metrics. Your redlines reduced latency targets and added tighter uptime commitment with monetary credits. Our standard SLA is 99.9% for hosted API with credits scaling by downtime, and we have a separate SLA for Dedicated with a higher uptime target.
[03:32] Sophie Larsen: Given our regulatory needs and customer SLAs we can't absorb frequent blips. We're asking for 99.95 for critical routes and a 50ms p95 target for short prompt flows, with credits if you miss p95 more than three times a month.
[03:50] Omar Patel: Ok — two things: 50ms p95 is aggressive depending on model choice and sequence length. For Redwood Dedicated or Private deployments pinned to smaller models it's more achievable. For hosted multi-tenant API with large models p95 tends to be higher. There's always a tradeoff latency vs cost.
[04:10] Noah Rivera: We're willing to budget for dedicated capacity if that gets us the targets. We just need a predictable price.
[04:18] Maya Chen: Makes sense. We can map your critical routes to Dedicated with a pricing appendix for reserved capacity. Pricing approval for that tier usually requires executive sign-off. Sophie, what's your procurement timeline?
[04:30] Sophie Larsen: We want procurement wrapped by end of month, but legal redlines could push. If we can get an updated MSA this week and a clear committed pricing sheet, we can likely make a decision.
[04:45] Ethan Park: On pricing, can you give a ballpark for the Reserved Capacity commit and any uplift for Private deployment? We need that to present to finance.
[04:55] Maya Chen: Ballpark — Dedicated pools start at a monthly commit equivalent to ~40k USD for the entry tier that meets medium throughput. Private (VPC/on-prem) has a platform fee plus infra; typical enterprise deals land around 80k-150k monthly depending on hardware sizing. I'll put numbers in the pricing appendix.
[05:12] Priya Menon: We will need an itemized TCO comparison — hosted vs dedicated vs private — including expected per-token cost at estimated throughput.
[05:22] Maya Chen: We'll send a TCO worksheet. Omar, can we include a model suggestion and quantization profile to hit the latency target while keeping cost reasonable?
[05:30] Omar Patel: Yes, we'll recommend quantized variants and batching configurations; for the 50ms p95 use-case we might suggest a smaller LLM variant or custom compilation settings. Also prefix/KV cache helps if your queries have repetition.
[05:45] Ethan Park: Back to legal — indemnity and regulatory obligations. There's a clause about regulatory fines; we need to ensure Redwood will assist with investigations and provide logs/audit trails. Also SOC 2 evidence and an option for an on-site audit?
[06:05] Maya Chen: We provide SOC 2 Type II reports and can provide tailored audit support. On-site audits for Private deployments are possible under enterprise agreements. We'll add an audit-support clause to the MSA appendix.
[06:18] Sophie Larsen: Great. Also SSO and RBAC — we need SAML-based SSO and role mapping to ensure separation of duties.
[06:27] Omar Patel: We support SAML and SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC in the console. I'll attach a quick integration checklist.
[06:36] Noah Rivera: Do you have docs on acceptable data residency regions? We have EU-only requirements for a subset of customers.
[06:44] Maya Chen: Yes, we support EU regions and can do Private in region; will confirm the exact EU locations supported and add to the DPA.
[06:52] Ethan Park: About subprocessors — we want a 30-day notice and a right to object for any new subprocessor that would process regulated financial data.
[07:02] Omar Patel: We can add a notice period and an objection process; if objection isn't resolvable, we can discuss mitigation like routing to Private deployment.
[07:12] Sophie Larsen: Ok. Next — breach notification timelines. Our policy requires 72 hours for regulator notification readiness.
[07:20] Ethan Park: 72 hours is standard for us. Can Redwood commit to 72-hour initial notification?
[07:26] Maya Chen: We typically notify within 72 hours for confirmed incidents; we'll commit to initial notification within 72 hours for incidents affecting regulated data, subject to reasonable investigation. I'll check legal language to make it crisp.
[07:40] Sophie Larsen: Good. One outstanding technical ask — we want a quick end-to-end benchmark: private deployment with our workload and a representative prompt set, measure p95 and throughput. If that passes, we can accelerate approval.
[07:55] Omar Patel: We can run a 3-day benchmark on a dedicated private tenant. We'll need a test spec from Priya and a small dataset and expected concurrency patterns.
[08:06] Priya Menon: I'll prepare the test spec. What do you need for network peering and firewall rules?
[08:12] Omar Patel: For Private in customer VPC we'll need peering details, allowed CIDR, and service endpoints. I'll send a checklist.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Great. So action plan: Redwood sends updated MSA with proposed liability cap increase and SLA language, Omar shares KMS/HSM and subnet/peering checklist, Aurora shares test spec and data residency list.
[08:34] Ethan Park: One more — pricing approval workflow. Who signs off on dedicated capacity? Is it AE or requires commercial/legal?
[08:42] Maya Chen: Pricing above a certain threshold routes to commercial ops; for this deal I'll pull in our pricing ops. We'll produce a definitive pricing appendix for you to take to finance.
[08:55] Sophie Larsen: Ok. Any competitor specifics we should call out? We've been asked why Redwood vs CloudGiant AI — main concern was their lower latency claims.
[09:05] Omar Patel: CloudGiant tends to optimize for low-latency use-cases but often with closed models; Redwood's advantage is flexible deployment options, open model catalog, and measurable unit economics. If you want, we can run a head-to-head benchmark plan.
[09:20] Noah Rivera: That could help. If we can see objective numbers we can justify the extra cost for dedicated capacity.
[09:28] Maya Chen: We'll include a benchmark/scorecard template in the follow-up.
[09:34] Ethan Park: Back to DPA — data subject requests and deletion. We need a clear deletion and retention clause, and ability to export logs in machine readable format.
[09:46] Omar Patel: We have retention settings and APIs for export. For multi-tenant hosted API there are retention defaults; in Dedicated and Private you can set shorter retention. We'll document the API endpoints.
[09:58] Sophie Larsen: Good. Any other legal blockers?
[10:02] Ethan Park: The arbitration clause — we prefer courts in our jurisdiction. We can discuss but may accept neutral arbitration.
[10:10] Maya Chen: We'll take that back to legal. Often customers and Redwood agree on neutral arbitration or specific jurisdiction for enterprise.
[10:18] Sophie Larsen: Ok. Timeline recap?
[10:22] Maya Chen: We'll aim to get the updated MSA and pricing appendix to you by 2026-12-22. You review redlines by 2026-12-28. We'll run the 3-day benchmark early Jan and reconvene 2027-01-05 to finalize pricing and onboarding. Does that fit?
[10:40] Sophie Larsen: Yes, that works for Aurora.
[10:44] Priya Menon: I'll send the test spec by 2026-12-23 and the list of KMS providers we need by the same day.
[10:52] Maya Chen: Perfect. Anything else?
[10:55] Ethan Park: No, thanks — please include SOC 2 and any ISO docs in the package.
[11:01] Maya Chen: Will do. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and next steps.

End of transcript.

References/shared artifacts noted during call: pricing appendix draft link: https://redwood.docs/pricing/aurora-draft, MSA redlines shared in Doc, benchmarking spec template will be shared, SOC 2 report link to be provided.

Action items (re-iterated):
- Maya Chen: Send updated MSA and pricing appendix (due 2026-12-22)
- Ethan Park: Provide DPA redlines and list of KMS providers (due 2026-12-23)
- Omar Patel: Send private deployment checklist and benchmark test spec template (due 2027-01-03)
